maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening at ten o'clock I had just started to speak on the supply motion, particularly with reference to agriculture. In review I might say that I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks that in order to have a healthy agricultural economy, not only has it to be healthy in western Canada but it must also be healthy in eastern Canada. You cannot have two distinct programs; you must have one national program.
I was dealing particularly with an important question. I said that I did not think we should be critical unless we would be constructive. I pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture through you, Mr. Speaker-and I am glad to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his seat today-that with Russia we had one of the most economic contracts for the sale of western wheat which we ever had, outside of the one with China. I said to the minister that I thought it was regrettable we did not have the facilities in

Eastern Agricultural Assistance this country, particularly the railway facilities-I wonder whether we could have a little order, Mr. Speaker?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Order, please. I am finding it very difficult to hear the interesting remarks of the hon. member.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Coming back to what I was saying, it is rather regrettable that a country which favours not only an agricultural industry but also an industrial economy did not have the facilities either through the railroads or at our ports or otherwise to move grain to Russia. When this government was elected they said they were going to be a government of action, and I maintain that if they had got busy with the railroads and the farm organizations, the pools of western Canada and the line companies which purchase our grain at local elevator level, and make certain those facilities were such as to move the grain off western Canadian farms, we could have supplied the grain to Russia instead of letting the United States do it. When these negotiations were first entered into the United States was against selling wheat to those people who were living behind the iron curtain. It was only after we were unable to complete our contract or fulfil the demands of Russia that the United States stepped into the picture and was able to take a big slice of the contract which might have gone to the farmers of western Canada.
My charge to the government is that although the wheat board has done a good job and has co-operated throughout the years to sell grain for the western farmers, this government has been irresponsible in that it did not get the facilities ready to deliver that grain. As I said last night, I maintain that when the law of supply and demand operates then there is prosperity on the farms of Canada, whether they be in western Canada or in eastern Canada.
I think the main reason these facilities were not ready was the position taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when the government first took office. What was that position? I set it out very clearly last evening. The position was that the government told the farmers of western Canada that the former minister of agriculture, who is in his place today and who told the farmers to grow grain so they could meet the demands of Russia and China, was "all wet". They said that the farmers should not have been encouraged to grow grain because there would be a large surplus.
I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press for September 23 last so as to put the exact words on the record. Under the
[Mr. WoolUams.l
heading "Wheat curb urged" the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture are reported as follows:
Mr. Sharp said the Soviet sale did not change the advice he gave last spring that Canadian farmers should grow less wheat and more of other kinds of crops.
Mr. Hays said farmers should cut their wheat acreage and turn to crops like feed grains. A 10 per cent reduction in wheat acreage, he said, would put Canadian wheat production back in the 500 million bushels a year range-
In other words those two ministers took the position that even with a contract with Russia and a contract with China there was going to be a surplus of grain. The fact is that if we had fulfilled the contract that Russia would have liked to sign with this country, fulfilled the obligation with Russia under the contract we already had, and had had the facilities to deliver this grain, there would have been a great boom in the agricultural industry of this country.
I do not know how the minister can now reconcile his position. He was shortsighted. He was irresponsible. He was not aware of the situation when he spoke to the farmers on that occasion, not only in Edmonton but in Moose Jaw and throughout western Canada. I should like to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture explain their positions.
Today they would like to take the credit. I noticed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce went to Los Angeles recently. I do not know whether he was in Hollywood, but he made a speech claiming that these large wheat sales which he was putting through were a great thing. When we on this side of the house were on the other side of the house we were told these contracts were the wheat board's contracts. He was the one who criticized them, who told the farmers to produce smaller crops; and today, of course, now that we have a boom they are endeavouring to take the credit for it. I do not think he will be able to pull the blinds over the eyes of the western farmers. I do not think Mr. Buckwold, the mayor of Saskatoon, will ever get into the cabinet, because the people of western Canada will know exactly what the situation is. I suppose because they have tried to bribe the voters before they will try to bribe them again, but it would seem to me that the people of Saskatoon, and particularly the farmers surrounding that area, will know the true picture and will know who really implemented a national agricultural policy in this country.
I ask the Minister of Agriculture, who has done a lot of travelling since he took that portfolio, to stand in his place when I have finished talking and name one piece of useful legislation he has placed on the statute

books for the farmers. The answer is that he has placed nothing on the statute books. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the wheat board has served the farmers well, but as far as the grain growers and agriculture are concerned, this government are most irresponsible. I am laying before the house the facts about this government this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that if any member of the house wishes to take the attitude that the hon. member for Bow River has taken, that is his privilege, and I have no recourse but to accept his statement. If I may continue with the wheat export figures, the all time high was 408 million bushels in the year 1928-29. To date we have exported 418 million bushels and we have two and a half more months to go. A year ago at the same time our exports were 255 million bushels. Remember those figures; 255 million bushels a year ago compared with 418 million bushels now.
I remember being on the west coast shortly after the Minister of Trade and Commerce made his visit there, when we learned that we must do something about the static condition in so far as shipments of wheat from the west coast were concerned. At that time the all time high was the unloading of 400 cars a day. It was not long before we had it up to 450 cars a day. We thought that was excellent. We were even more pleased when it reached 500 cars a day. We never thought it would get to 600 cars, but it has reached 650 cars a day.
By the first of August this year we will probably have exported in the neighbourhood of 600 million bushels of wheat. Add to this the 155 million bushels consumed in Canada and we come out with a figure of 755 million bushels. The all time high production was 723 million bushels of wheat last year. I think that pretty well takes care of the facts of the case, and I believe this government should be commended on the good job it has done. I am sure every farmer in Canada feels exactly the same way as the Russians, Chinese and other recipients of our grain.
The hon. member for Kootenay West made the comment last night that he now has a prize bull named Harry. I think that probably is a good name to give him if he is an active chap, and he probably is. At three o'clock this morning I telephoned the Minister of Forestry to ask him whether he wanted to come back to protect his ARDA program. He said "I do not think it will be necessary. All the farmers know about it, so I think I will not come back." My wife said to me, "To whom are you talking"? 1 said I had been talking to Sauve.
I said I was thinking about what the member for Kootenay West had said about me. I said "You remember the time we imported that highland cow from Scotland for which we paid $1,800". She had a bull calf and we took the bull calf back to western Canada. We did not want to expose him to any of the females and we did the necessary thing so that if he did jump the fence nothing would happen. We got to like him. He was
Eastern Agricultural Assistance a funny fellow. He was a little shaggy and did not do much, but we laughed at him. I said to my wife "I have been thinking that maybe we should call him Herbert, or Bert for short". She said "Well, I think that is a pretty good idea, but as he is such a nice, kindly old man why don't you call him after the old goat we have to keep the bulls from fighting?"
As Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker, I wish as nearly as possible to answer all the questions that were raised yesterday concerning the Department of Agriculture, because farming is a very serious business. We have a great responsibility to the farmers of Canada, and 1 do not think we should take it lightly. I want to answer what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said about feed grains. My colleague the hon. member for Kings mentioned the matter, but I should like to go into a little more detail.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to the feed grain policy which he said the previous government was ready to introduce at the time of the dissolution of parliament in 1963. I discussed the problem with farm organizations and found that they wanted a program which would ensure adequate supplies of feed grains in the east at prices which would not be affected by the close of navigation. I did not take long to appreciate that a program could readily be set up to do this very thing. The policy was announced on August 22, four months after we took office.
This was the policy under which the government reimbursed holders of western feed grains in eastern position for the winter carrying charges. As a result of this policy there were 30.8 million bushels of western oats, barley and feed wheat in eastern elevators at the close of navigation last year compared with 21.2 million bushels at the close of navigation in 1962, an increase of 9 million bushels. On May 13 this year there were 8.7 million bushels in eastern position compared with 6.7 million bushels a year ago.
I tabled in the house previously figures showing the manner in which this policy resulted in western feed grain prices staying uniform throughout the whole winter. The figures I tabled and which I am going to repeat now were assembled from the actual invoices of sales which are filed with the department under the freight assistance policy. These show that from October last year to April this year the average weighted price at Montreal of oats and barley shipped to retailers changed hardly at all. In October last year it was $2.44 per hundredweight for oats, and over the succeeding months it

Eastern Agricultural Assistance has varied from a low of $2.42, which was in April, to a high of $2.47. This is a very minor spread, I am sure.
The same thing has happened with barley prices. The average weighted wholesale price of barley, based again on the actual claims filed with the department, was $2.48 per hundredweight last October. The price in the succeeding months has never gone above that and, in fact, in April it was only $2.38.
Without this storage assistance policy it is very doubtful if we would have had the volume of feed grains in eastern Canada which we did have during the past winter and, based on previous years, we could have expected by April an increase of 17 cents a hundredweight in the price of oats compared to last fall and an increase of 13 cents in the price of barley, based on storage charges alone, plus any changes that may have occurred in the market due to short supplies.
Present indications are that this assistance policy will cost about $1 million, and I may say that this has been money very well spent because, in addition to the benefits which I have just reviewed, eastern and British Columbia livestock and poultry producers have used approximately 500,000 tons more Canadian feed grains this past year than they did during the previous year.
We have heard a great deal from the official opposition about what they intended to do about an eastern feed grain policy, but the fact is that nothing was done. The steps taken by this government last summer have contributed very substantially to improving both the supply position and the stabilization of prices over the winter months. This has been accomplished despite the very heavy pressure on both supplies and facilities occasioned by the immense overseas wheat movement.
The former minister of agriculture mentioned something about dairy policy. However, before I deal with dairy policy, I may say he referred to the fact that the previous government had a whole agriculture policy. I have been through the office and I have been through every drawer, but I cannot find it. If they had one they have taken it away with them, because I cannot find it.
As I say, the former minister mentioned dairy products. Several times during agricultural debates here it has been charged that savings have been made in the cost of the dairy support program at the expense of the dairy farmer. Any examination of the facts will show that this is not the case, but rather the moves that have been made have been a rationalization of the program with a transfer of part of the costs from the taxpayer to the actual buyer of the products. The only exception to this was the step

taken a year ago, a step which had been forecast by the previous government, to reduce the assistance previously given to fluid milk producers. Even here certain measures taken have been of assistance to this part of the industry.
To put this matter in perspective, let us look at the suggestion which has been made here that the $3.5 million saving which has been forecast this year will be at the expense of producers. This is obviously incorrect, since the support levels have not been changed and the $3.5 million represents entirely the saving of 1 cent per pound in the butter subsidy. Perhaps the best indication of the effects which the program changes have had on farmers' returns is the farm gate milk and butterfat prices recorded by the bureau of statistics. For the most recent month available, which is February, the average farm value of butterfat this year was 69.4 cents per pound, up 1.9 cents from a year ago. Cheese milk was $2.87 per hundredweight, up 7 cents from last year. Milk for concentration and ice cream was $2.85, up 15 cents from a year ago.
It has been suggested that changing the cheese subsidy from 30 cents per hundredweight of milk to 3.6 cents per pound for first grade Cheddar cheese is a backward step and that it will reduce producer returns. For Canada as a whole, based on the per cent of first grade cheese produced and the average yield per hundredweight of milk, the 3.6 cents subsidy is equivalent to 30.5 cents per hundredweight of milk. While it is true that there are some plants whose production of first grade cheese is below the national average, I am confident that the present program will provide an incentive to improve cheese quality and will provide a basis for the payment to producers for cheese milk on a quality basis. I think it is important to point out that there are cheese factories which consistently produce less than 60 per cent first grade cheese.
Some members have suggested that a lowering of the export assistance on cheese would adversely affect our markets abroad. Changes in the export assistance have only been made as market conditions in the importing countries warranted it. Last year the assistance on cheese was reduced by 1 cent and export markets absorbed this difference. Exports last dairy year were 31.2 million pounds compared to 27.4 million pounds the year before.
I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle that we have not yet reached a final solution in regard to a dairy policy. It does seem to me, however, that rising producer returns, increasing consumption, greater exports and decreasing stocks are a distinct

improvement over the mounting surpluses which faced us when we came into office.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to a water policy for eastern Canada similar to the P.F.R.A. in western Canada. Under ARDA we have been carrying forward an aggressive water policy in eastern Canada. In Quebec we have entered into agreements with the province for 82 drainage and channel improvement projects at a total cost to the federal government of $1,169,000. I might say that this is almost the amount that had been spent on this program in all the previous years. In Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick we are participating with the provinces in community and farm pond programs and in open ditch drainage and channel improvement projects. The total contribution to these projects by the federal government to date is $223,000. In Ontario we are participating in a complete soil and conservation project for the Whiteman creek watershed which is part of the area coming under the Grand river conservation authority. The total contribution to this project is $223,000.
In addition to these active conservation programs we are engaged in several water resources projects. We are doing a ground water resource inventory in the Annapolis valley of Nova Scotia and in the Big creek watershed in Norfolk county in Ontario. We have a project which is being carried out by the Ontario water resources commission for a surface of water resources survey in irrigation and other rural uses in southwestern Ontario. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the engineering assistance of M.M.R.A. is being redirected to cover a comprehensive watershed protection and development plan for the Musquodoboit river in Nova Scotia and the Kennebecasis river in New Brunswick.
The hon. member also mentioned that he had planned a livestock policy. It is my contention that the most immediate need of the Canadian livestock industry is to put itself in a position to better meet competition, both internally and abroad. This, I believe, can best be done through increasing the efficiency of our basic flocks and herds, whether by decreasing the amount of feed required to produce a pound of beef, a pound of pork, a dozen eggs or a pound of chicken, or by increasing the rate of gain of the animals or rate of lay of the birds.
The approach to this problem is manyfold, but fundamental to it all is the need for active, accurate and expanding testing programs. Canada has always had an excellent record of performance program for dairy cattle. I should like to digress here a little by stating that 42 countries recognize that
Eastern Agricultural Assistance Canada has the finest dairy cattle in the world. They have recognized this for something like 40 years. I come back now to the fact that Canada has always had an excellent record of performance program for dairy cattle. On taking office we were confronted with a backlog of applications from 115 farmers who, because of the staffing situation within the record of performance organization, were unable to avail themselves of this excellent program. This was immediately corrected.
Testing programs must, however, be reinforced and complemented by research programs having in mind the over-all objectives that I have just outlined. In order to do this we are reassessing the emphasis in livestock and poultry research programs. A further step in such a national program is to ensure that the benefits that can accrue from such programs are brought rapidly and strongly to the attention of livestock producers. Possibly the best forum for this would be the many fairs and exhibitions at which livestock of all classes are exhibited.
Over the years livestock classifications have tended to move away from utility factors. A definite step has been taken to reorient livestock classifications through the establishment for the current year of a pilot project at certain fairs. This project will provide the basis for a major change in the assistance program to fairs and exhibitions and will ensure that utility and efficiency assume their rightful place in the evaluation of our livestock.
Now, Mr. Speaker, another project which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle mentioned as having been in his party's plans, but which had not been introduced, was a fertilizer policy. As hon. members know, there are some agricultural matters which are attended to by the federal government and some which are attended to by the provinces. Matters such as fertilizer assistance have always been regarded as a field of provincial activity. The province of Quebec has had a fertilizer assistance program for a number of years, on which they spend between $2.5 million and $3 million annually.
There have been suggestions from time to time in the house that much more is being done for western agriculture than for eastern agriculture. I think it would be desirable to put some figures on the record to illustrate that these suggestions are not correct. For example, in the fiscal year 1963-64 payments under the various deficiency payment programs of the agricultural stabilization board totalled $31.8 million in eastern Canada and $10.3 million in western Canada. On butterfat alone, Quebec farmers received $14.3 million and Ontario farmers $9.6 million, which is a

On the international level, Senator Y. Here is what he says on page 2 of his brief:
Better means of communication, automobile, radio, television, some progress (still not enough of course) towards equal education, have brought about clashes between agriculture and the other sectors of the economy. The rise of labour unions, co-operatives or mutual associations has shown the young farmers the value of number and the strength derived from unity and sometimes its corollary: the use of force to gain satisfaction.
Of course, it is not those indications at the international level which will remedy the

situation here. In our part of the country, in the east and especially in the province of Quebec, a revolution is going in our farming communities which, in days past, formed an autonomous parochial economy and tried to be self-sufficient. However, the advent of such means of communication as the radio, television and newspapers and the opening of roads have created completely different problems.
Nowadays, young farmers are no longer satisfied with living on the farm as their forefathers did; they want to enjoy all the advantages of modern society. But, at the same time, it is no longer as easy for them to be self-sufficient because they must take the money they make from the sale of their production to buy the consumer and other goods necessary to satisfy his needs.
It is there that is felt the great difference between the standard of living in industrialized areas and the one existing in farming areas. They are conscious of that fact and they are shocked.
We are witnessing-and you know it-an economic concentration in about 15 large cities across the country and a constant exodus of young men and women from rural areas. This is obviously creating serious economic, social and moral problems.
Those economic problems often force young men and women getting nowhere in their own areas to leave for the larger centres. They are faced with difficult problems because they are ill-prepared to earn a living and to contribute by their work to the normal development of the community in which they live.
On the other hand, the rural communities where this social haemorrhage is taking place are affected by the loss of their young men and women who could, if they had the opportunity to do so, contribute by their vitality, their energy and their work to the development of their community.
From a social and local point of view, we must remember that this emptying of all those parishes creates many serious problems, since people remaining have to pay for education, schools and local organizations, and they often are left with only the young and the old people, while those who could develop the community through their vitality and their work have to go elsewhere.
There is no need for me to emphasize the moral significance of this uprooting of people who, sometimes ill-prepared, in an environment unsuitable to them where they feel like strangers, encounter difficulties of all kinds for their own moral life.
Of course, the family is the natural basis of society; it is the mother-cell of society.
Eastern Agricultural Assistance We shall not add to our moral or to our material wealth by destroying the soundest cells of our society. Unfortunately, we sometimes see this evil developing like a cancer through an irrational and rapid development of certain sectors, thus destroying the healthier cells of our society.
This creates a number of problems for the underdeveloped areas which are asking for the tools that would further their development.
However, in accordance with the philosophy of economic liberalism, the first condition which is laid down is that it must be an economically sound proposition. Since that condition is not fulfilled, these areas are sometimes refused the tools which would contribute to lift them up from their economic misery.
I say that the agricultural problem has not only one solution in the remedies related to agriculture itself. The present government has put on the order paper a number of measures just waiting to be passed. Perhaps a greater contribution would be made by letting that legislation to be passed as quickly as possible rather than moving want of confidence motions.
I will not go into the details of all those measures. The minister himself explained them and other speakers have indicated to what extent the present government intends to contribute to the financing of farm properties or agricultural institutes, to assist farmers by means of a support price for milk, butter and other commodities and do some planning in the case of products that are difficult to sell, in short, how the government wants to encourage the production of other commodities which would boost our exports.
But I want to point out the fact that we will not find a definite solution to the farm problems without looking after the development of the whole territory of a region. And that is when the whole problem of an improved economic balance throughout the country arises: the need to bring back on their feet the distressed areas and to assist, as the present government is doing, those distressed areas which are grouping themselves and want to contribute to the solution of their problems.
Neither will there be one easy utopian solution for the farm problem. We shall have to group ourselves according to the various areas to find the true avocation of our communities and invite the whole population to work hard at its own development. And I would say that it is up to the communities to take the initiative and start this necessary economic re-grouping, with the assistance of local authorities and later, of the provincial and federal governments.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
The point of knowing whether the matter of designating areas was under federal jurisdiction has been much discussed. Where were those who wondered whether this did not come under provincial jurisdiction. As for me, I say that we live under a democratic system and that it is, first of all, up to the various areas to group themselves and have those groups recognized by the higher authorities, taking into consideration the avocation and trend of the collectivities and have their suggestions approved by the higher authorities of this country, keeping, of course, in mind the latter's recommendations in this field.
There will have to be agreements to proceed with the inventory of our communities and at the same time projects will have to be started to make people wait patiently for the implementation of fully considered, long term schemes; it will be necessary also to canalize the clearly expressed local ambitions and hopes while neither minimizing nor spuming such hopes by trying to implement over-simplified solutions.
I say, borrowing Boussuet's words: "It is among the people that you will find plain common sense".
One has to attend the meetings of the economic guidance council of the lower St. Lawrence to see how interested our people are, how devoted and ready to co-operate in their own economic development.
But alone they will not be able to go against the very strong current I have mentioned before if they do not receive that sympathy which is given to a sick child who gets not only the medicine it needs but also the best food to restore him to health.
I do not accept the principle according to which, the rentability being the same, preference will be given to the setting up of industries in depressed areas.
It is like telling two children one of whom is healthy and the other crippled; first come first served. In such a way, the former would surely get fatter and the latter would only get weaker.
If economics only is laid down as basic principle, the vicious circle by which more is given to those who have already a lot, and nothing to those who do not have much, will be further emphasized.
However, if this principle of economics is not taken into consideration, this will open the door to numerous abuses. Hence the need, in order to intervene effectively, for area planning and justification for the creation of a rural development department. That is another government measure, which followed the establishment of the economic council and the Department of Industry, as well as the

adoption of a group of other pieces of legislation, designed to relieve underdeveloped areas, which proves the sincerity of the present government in its endeavour to better the lot of underdeveloped areas, especially the farmers.
It will be quite a challenge and quite a task for the department to put an end to unemployment in rural areas and, at the same time, to develop that territory, to set up industries related to agriculture-we will have to come to that if we are to provide a market for our agricultural products-and to process forest products locally. As forestry engineers pointed out in their brief to the Belanger commission, because there are no other resources, trees are being cut indiscriminately and forests are being spoiled to pay land taxes and other taxes whereas what we need at present is a long term reforestation policy.
The paradoxical situation of sailors throwing cargo overboard to save the ship is not uncommon. However, if we have set up an economic council, a Department of Industry, designated areas-the criteria and statistics used for the establishment of such areas should be revised-and the responsibility to deal with those problems, which they could not do successfully, will not rest only with that department but rather with all the departments, all the crown corporations and all governments at every level.
Individuals in society are not like potatoes in a bag. The rotten potato can be taken out to prevent it from corrupting the others. We know that society is constituted like the various limbs of the human body, in such a way that if one of those limbs gets sick, and if it is not nursed in time, the whole body is in danger. Therefore, we cannot be satisfied with global statistics and we must see to it that adequate remedies are applied to the affected limbs.
It is therefore necessary that all departments and all crown corporations be not partitioned, but agree that they can, while administering in the best possible way their own department, work in such a way that an appropriate decentralization should provide for the rehabilitation of areas which could, not only take care of themselves, but contribute to the general development of the country.
I say that, in any case, we will have to pay the bill for the progress or the recession, and we have no alternative. I think it is more pleasant and more profitable to supply the required tools, the organization which is essential to the development of resources, and invest the money required for that purpose, or else the number of those who

have no other alternative but the welfare state will increase and we shall revert to what caused the decline of Rome, when demagogues were promising bread and games, leading to believe that a people can unduly live on empty dreams, sponging on the whole world, and keeping the nation in the dream of a marvellous world where we could get rid forever of all the miserable people who stemmed that sea of hidden and miraculous plenty which could spread over suffering mankind and bathe everybody in a sea of joy and plenty.
It must be recalled, Mr. Speaker, that if the 30 acres of ice and snow have become a huge and rich country-the second nation in the world as far as exports and industry are concerned-it is certainly not because we have one of the most favourable or easy climates. It must be recalled that other nations, other countries had just like us abundant natural resources and a milder climate.
But, if we have the development by which we are benefiting today, it is because we had serious, hard-working and honest people and governments that could inspire confidence to the whole world.
We must do our share to maintain that confidence to support initiatives, encourage capital investments in the development of our natural resources while not giving away, of course, our right to control our economy and our policy. We must create the climate necessary to the birth of the great undertakings which have made of our country, in spite of great handicaps, such as distance, climate and remoteness, one of the most prosperous in the world.
Of course, that psychological climate does not just happen, it follows action taken by a responsible government, seconded by understanding and support by a people proud of its freedom and anxious to contribute, in a climate of confidence, to the normal evolution of its social, economic and political life.
That is why, notwithstanding the stand taken by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent), I will support the present government with regard to its farm policy and I will give it my confidence tonight because it is creating, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, a climate of confidence which might give new life to our country's economy. Well, I do not pretend to be the great authority on agriculture that the hon. member may be, but at least I happen to be standing on my feet in the House of Commons and he happens to be sitting in his place, as he has been doing all through this debate. At least I am making an effort to put forward a contribution which will be of some assistance to farmers and to those associated with agriculture in eastern Canada.
I go back to 1962, to the election campaign of that year, and in particular to a meeting which was attended by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who was then minister of agriculture. He spoke in my constituency and at that time he outlined a six point program for agriculture in eastern Canada. During that meeting my hon. friend read from the statements he made in western Canada. Those statements were the same as the statements he made in eastern Canada. He was a minister who had a good appreciation of the problems of agriculture across this country. At that time he said our government would go forward and take special steps to correct the inequities which could not be overcome by national legislation. He told the people of eastern Canada what he was endeavouring to do as minister of agriculture and as a member of the Progressive Conservative government to correct the inequities which needed to be corrected if agriculture in eastern Canada was to have a healthy future.
After the election campaign we came back to Ottawa as the party forming the government, and among the statements contained in the speech from the throne presented to that new parliament was the following:
The prosperity of agriculture remains essential to the well-being of the entire Canadian economy. Canada is blessed this year with very large crops of good quality, and export markets for Canadian agricultural products have been very greatly enlarged.
My ministers recognize that livestock is occupying a position of increasing importance in Canadian agriculture. They propose that a program be instituted to ensure the availability of storage facilities and continuity of supplies of feed grain to match the expanding requirements for livestock production, particularly in the areas of British Columbia and eastern Canada where supplies of feed grain are normally deficient.
Before that session ended-and it did not end because we asked that it should end, but because the combined opposition voted that parliament out of existence-the minister of agriculture had his legislation ready. He was ready to move, and move quickly, in an endeavour to eliminate the inequities which he knew existed in agriculture in eastern Canada.

Another election campaign ensued. The promises made during the 1962 campaign were reaffirmed. We were not re-elected as a government-

Mr. Suderman writes:

Stacked against these measures of relatively minor importance is the Liberal record in wheat sales which prevented the government's performance in agriculture from being viewed as a complete disaster.
The Liberal record in agriculture was hardly helped by the legacies of the last two election campaigns. None of the Liberal farm planks have been adopted and many have been dropped. The two-dollar guarantee on wheat won few adherents in the west and was quickly and quietly buried. The promise of an east-west ministry of agriculture has also been dropped despite claims to the contrary. The proposal to make support payments on eggs quarterly and regionally was dropped. The promised feed grain program, which included subsidized loans to co-op built storages, also did not make its appearance. The school milk programs, improvements to the crop insurance program, expansion in farm credit facilities-all promises of the "63 campaign"-could show up in the present commons session.
The three-way split in agriculture responsibilities opens the government to cross-examination by the opposition. When Mr. Hays was reported to be in opposition to a buying and selling feed grain board, questions were immediately directed at Mr. Sauve and Prime Minister Pearson. Was Mr. Hays speaking for the government? Neither Mr. Sauve nor Mr. Pearson was able to answer. Sources close to cabinet were equally unclear. Some said that Mr. Hays was obviously expressing government policies. Others, pointing to Mr. Sauve's
Eastern Agricultural Assistance plans to study the question again, said there was no policy for or against such a board. Who is right?
Well, with regard to agriculture a great many people have asked that question ever since this government took office. Who knows what is going on in agriculture? Today we see one of the three ministers in his seat in the house. Where are the other two? Can we be certain that any statements which one of them may make will be corroborated by the other two. I, for one, had hoped that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) would be in his place today, in view of the fact that he recently made a tour of ARDA installations in the Atlantic provinces. I was hopeful he would make a statement so that we might have some idea of his future plans for ARDA in the maritime provinces.
But he is not here. We do not know whether we may accept what the Minister of Agriculture has to say with regard to ARDA in view of the fact that he no longer has responsibility for that program. But I will say this, Mr. Speaker, that never has there been a greater indication that one man should be responsible for our agricultural policies in this country than since this government took office. No one knows what the other fellow is doing. But we all know this, that the government are not doing very much, if anything, except marking time and throwing out smokescreens rather than providing policies, action and helpful measures which will be of benefit to agriculture.
Yesterday the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) put before the government a six-point program and asked them to give very serious consideration to it. I should like to add one specific item to the program of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and I ask the government whether they would give consideration to it. I have a constituency which is one of the best grassed constituencies in Canada. We could be producing a great deal more livestock than is evident today. One of the problems we face is that while we have some very excellent farm operations in existence there are too many marginal farm operations and vacant farms which could be utilized in a very efficient manner if the right type of individual was operating them. I have noticed over the years that the Dutch immigrants who have come into this country and who occupy many of the farms in my constituency have made a tremendous success of their operation. I would hope that the Minister of Agriculture would urge the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) to do his very best to see whether he could attract more Dutch immigrants to the maritimes to take over these vacant farms and once again make them operative.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
Another of the problems which we encounter in my part of Canada is that a great many of the farmers are older men whose sons have grown up and probably secured a good or a satisfactory education; an education sufficient to allow them to go to the bigger cities, the bigger population areas of this country, and secure jobs in factories and things of that type. The situation we see is that no matter how much credit we might make available and no matter how lucrative we might make it for farmers to accept the credit available, they are not going to accept it because there is no one on the farm willing to assume the obligations, should illness befall the farmer who is presently operating it. In view of this I think it is most urgent that we try by every means possible to interest young boys to stay with their fathers or to secure adjoining farmland so that they will continue to have an interest in agriculture and in the unit their parents are operating. In this way it may be possible to enlarge our holdings and to enlarge the livestock capacity of the farm.
It may be of some interest to note that when I placed a question on the order paper and asked for information about which programs were being carried out in Cumberland in relation to ARDA, I was told that the only one which had been finalized was one associated with the Minudie community pasture. There is another area in my constituency which should, in my opinion, be developed into a community pasture. It has been suggested that the east Amherst marsh could be developed into a wholly different type of community pasture from the one at Minudie in that different farmers in the area could be apportioned a certain acreage in that community pasture, and made responsible for its use. It would be available to them as long as they indicated an interest in, and a desire to improve and to use, that land. I put out those two suggestions as ones which might assist in bettering economic prospects in my constituency.
Now I should like to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) and to ask the minister whether he would explain the very apparent differences in the prices of oats, wheat and barley which were paid for these products when the policy of assistance was announced on April 22, compared with the price which the farmers were paid for the same products in the latter part of September. If the minister will look at the figures he will find that there was a tremendous increase in the cost of these products to the producer. The western producer did not receive this increase; the eastern producer paid for it. Where did the money go? There can only be one answer: it

went to someone other than the farmers in either eastern or western Canada. This was a state of affairs which the minister was supposed to eliminate by the policy he laid down in the order in council of August 22.
There has to be in my opinion a very substantial and determined program put forward by this government if it is to lift agriculture out of the doldrums it so evidently is in in the maritime provinces. There cannot be any piecemeal type of program. There has to be a concentrated program that touches every facet of agriculture. There is no evidence whatsoever, absolutely none, that this government is taking any substantial steps to do anything about our problems in eastern Canada in relation to agriculture or in relation to anything else. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) today asked a question of the Minister of Labour. He was asking this question as the result of a statement the minister made in St. Catharines, Ontario, to the effect that the only hope of any unemployed Canadian of finding work is to move to another part of the country, and the fare would be made available by the government. We heard this a long time ago in the Gordon report, and now we hear it from a Nova Scotian. It does not make it any more palatable because it comes from a Nova Scotian. It is what we told the people in our area would happen if this party were elected to office.

This is because this government have refused time and time again to take any action of any kind related to the Atlantic provinces, and in fact have eliminated some of the work we did have in relation to their defence policies.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude by reading a short editorial which appears in today's Ottawa Journal. I think it confirms what I have been saying regarding this government and the smokescreens it set up in place of action. This editorial is entitled "Blame is government's" and it says:
Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Douglas, who do not often agree, co-operated for a moment In the Commons the other day. They proved that the Liberal government wants to blame others for its own mistakes.
"Don't blame us for parliament being slow", the Liberals cry. "Blame the irresponsible opposition".
But see, on the 64th day of the present session, the Prime Minister giving a long list of business the government hopes to get through, as he said.

"before summer". Mr. Pearson asked for cooperation and brought from Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Douglas the reasonable objection that they had to know where co-operation was required before they could give it.
Mr. Diefenbaker commented there was little on the order paper to guide the official opposition on the government program and Mr. Douglas added: "One of the ways in which the government can discharge its responsibility is to get some of this legislation on the order paper so that members will have an opportunity to study it".
It is only a year since Mr. Pearson's cabinet- called "a cabinet of all the talents" by Liberal enthusiasts-took office. It has shown a persistent and distressing inability to manage the legislative program efficiently. The responsibility for inefficiency is the government's.
I make the final plea to the Minister of Agriculture to try and give the type of leadership, the type of hope and inspiration to the farmers of eastern Canada that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) gave them during the period in which he was minister of agriculture.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will endeavour not to refer to my notes any more than is absolutely necessary. I mentioned that the realized net income figures were more compatible to the hon. member. The cash income figures show an increase and are at an all time high. He quibbles about a small variation of .1 per cent in the increase between 1962 and 1963, that is, 2.2 compared with 2.1. Surely he must realize that the preliminary provincial totals were published in February and the final in May when further information for the year 1963 had become available.
In the report on cash income, No. 21-001, published on May 22 it was pointed out that the net income report would be published in about two weeks time. This net income report, as is the case each year, will present figures on realized net income and total net income from farming operations. An advanced preliminary statement for net income only was published in February.
Eastern Agricultural Assistance
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle drew particular attention to the net income figures indicating the wide variation between the year 1961 and 1963 in net income and comparisons of net with the realized net series. I am sure he is fully aware that the realized net income series does not take into account inventory changes. He also knows that Saskatchewan had a poor crop in 1961. Cash receipts and realized income levels were fairly well maintained because farmers sold accumulated carryovers of grain from previous crop years. The inventory adjustment, however, was quite large and therefore caused a sharp decline in the figure for total net income.
A word about these series. It will be apparent that the choice of one or the other will depend in large measure on the use or abuse to which people wish to put them. Series like these are produced by the United States and most developed nations of the world. Underdeveloped countries include them in their pressing need for statistical data.
As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle completed his address he referred to eastern agriculture and his amendment is based on the failure of the government to do anything about the problems of eastern agriculture. I want to thank him for being so charitable as to refer to this particular subject, because if we had been choosing a subject to suggest to the opposition as one on which they should propose a motion of non-confidence we would have suggested the program of the government with regard to eastern agriculture.
Some reference has been made to the needs of eastern agriculture. I think I am safe in saying that no group could be more sensitive to the needs of eastern agriculture than the present government. It was this particular sensitivity to the needs that caused the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to propose that a special minister, who would assume responsibility for ARDA and for some aspects of eastern agriculture, should be appointed. I am happy to say that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) has now visited every province in the country. He is currently visiting the prairie provinces. He was in Manitoba last night, is in Edmonton today and will be in Regina tomorrow.
The purpose of these visits is to ascertain the peculiar needs of the provinces with regard to rural development, and to assess the ways in which our ARDA program may be adapted to those respective provinces. It is the expectation of the minister, after this appraisal has been made, that amendments to the policy may be necessary. These will be presented in this house and the program

Eastern Agricultural Assistance will be proceeded with in order to meet the various needs of the provinces within this country.
It has been suggested that this government has not done anything for eastern agriculture. I suppose it would be reasonable to say that we must have a starting point, a point at which we commence to make our comparisons. I suppose such a date would be April 22 when this government assumed office. We all recall that within hours after assuming office a new dairy policy for Canada was put into effect. We all, of course, remember with some displeasure the mounting butter surplus which existed prior to April 22. We also know that there were substantial demands for cheese, for which we were not able to supply a suitable product. It was the opinion of the government, therefore, that there should be a new emphasis placed on the production of cheese and a declining emphasis placed on the production of butter. This was done within hours of this government's taking office.
I believe that today the minister indicated the extent to which this policy has been successful. For the first time since 1956, the production of butter and the consumption of butter are in line. As a matter of fact, there has been a deficit in production as compared with consumption. In addition, our cheese production is up approximately 18 per cent. I believe that if this government had done nothing else but institute the dairy policy that was instituted within hours after taking office, this would be a very commendable approach to agriculture problems in eastern Canada.
Then, too, it has been suggested nothing has been done, but within a few weeks of taking office a new feed grain policy was announced. This policy has done several things. It has assured eastern users of a constant supply of grain at all times. As a result, there has been an adequate supply of grain at all times through the winter which has resulted in a uniformity in price.
The minister referred to some of our livestock improvement works. He mentioned the r.o.p. policy in connection with dairy cattle. I should like to make some comparisons here because it is only by comparison we are able to indicate the extent to which this government is meeting the needs of eastern agriculture. When this government assumed office, as indicated by the minister, there were some 115 dairy farmers in Canada waiting to be accepted on r.o.p. lists. Within days, or within a very few weeks, the necessary provisions were made to enable these farmers to be serviced, and this program was put into full effect.

This is a worth-while policy. Canada is noted the world over for the excellence of her dairy cattle. This reputation has been built up over a substantial number of years as a result of careful selection based partly on the r.o.p. program. The former government, in the name of austerity, had issued a letter indicating that it was going to be necessary to cut down on this essential service to farmers and they would not be able to accept applications as they came in. The result was that, in order to save an estimated $250,000, this valuable service to farmers which has over the years kept the excellence of our dairy cattle at a very high level, was held in abeyance. This government immediately took action to institute a policy which has given a real lift to our r.o.p. program in this country.
Immediately after taking office the government dispatched a team of experts to Europe to study the swine industry for the purpose of discovering better methods of production, better techniques in feeding, and to bring back a report to this country. The recommendations of that team will be put into effect in a swine improvement policy for this country.
Within a short time of taking office, a new veterinary college was established in western Canada which will result in a general improvement in the health standards of our livestock. This, I believe, is a very commendable step. The minister mentioned the action that had been taken with regard to water policies and indicated that more had been undertaken since this government assumed office than had been undertaken for a number of years prior.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) suggested that this government has not fulfilled its mandate from the people. I want to suggest that in one year of administration you do not expect to be able to fulfil the mandate from the people. After all, this government has only been in power for one year and I have outlined a notable list of accomplishments that have been achieved by it. How can anyone ask the question, what has been done, when these things are obvious and are working to our mutual advantage?
Then, the Department of Agriculture has additional responsibilities. Not only is it concerned with the operation of these various policies which tend to keep the farmers solvent and agriculture in balance, but in addition the department has substantial responsibilities in connection with promoting research in order to improve our agriculture, in order that agriculture may better serve the farmers and provide better food at reasonable prices for the consuming public. I should like again to refer rather closely to the notes I

have before me in elaborating on a research program which will be proceeded with by this government.
The Canada Department of Agriculture seriously entered research with the establishment of five regional experimental farms in 1866. The primary task was to introduce the best of European agriculture in terms of plants and animals, select those best adapted to our conditions and learn how to manage them. Over the years, as our knowledge of our climate and soil has increased, more and more time has been devoted to developments specifically to meet Canadian conditions.
In so far as soils are concerned, for instance, originally we made progress, for example, in connection with fertility on a trial and error basis. Gradually we are learning more and more about our soils, their nature, their fertility, their response to drainage and irrigation. Today we are achieving some independence of soil through our ability to define its limitations in terms of the requirements of a particular crop and to manage it and supplement its fertility to provide an optimum medium for the crop. As our knowledge and understanding of our soils and of the nutrient requirements of each specific crop increase, we will come nearer and nearer to achieving independence from the soil. In other words, we will be able to manage the soil in such a way that it will not be a limiting factor in crop production. Unfortunately we cannot hope to achieve such control over temperature although we are making good progress towards ensuring adequate moisture.
With regard to plants, in the beginning we depended on varieties developed for conditions other than our own and were limited to selecting those which did best under Canadian conditions. Farmers paid little if any attention to variety, because oats were oats and timothy was timothy. Since we developed Marquis wheat specifically for our Canadian prairies we have gone ahead until today we have many varieties of cereals, forages and horticultural crops developed in Canada to meet the specific requirements of the farmer in a specific delineated area.
Each province makes annual variety recommendations on the basis of varieties tailored to its conditions. Farmers do not plant wheat, or timothy or alfalfa. They make their selections on the basis of specific recommended varieties. Tomorrow we will know much more about the requirements of specific crops in terms of light, of heat, of water, of nutrients and about the genetic make-up of plants in relation to the physiological response to environment and disease. The plant breeder will thus have the knowledge about 20220-229

Eastern Agricultural Assistance tailor-made varieties by direct selection of the genetic material which will carry the desired characters.
With regard to animals, in the early days we brought in European breeds of livestock and fed them on the feeds readily available on individual farms. There was no measure of efficiency in terms such as feed/grain ratios or profit factors. Through research we are gradually defining the nutrient requirements of stock for each stage of growth and production. We are developing techniques for evaluating and describing feed-stuffs in terms of what they will contribute toward these nutrient requirements. Today, our feed manufacturers and our farmers have been given considerable information for use in planning rations which will come close to exploiting the potential of a particular class of stock for growth or production. This information permits them to substitute individual ration components on a basis of current market prices and still meet nutrient requirements.
Today we are starting to accumulate new information on the profit factor in feeding high energy rations to meat and production classes of livestock, and are learning something about increasing the economy of maintaining and housing breeding herds and young stock prior to coming into production.

Our studies on non-pathological diseases such as bloat, acetonemia, and urinary calculi are giving or will give the anwers we need in devising management and feeding practices which will eliminate these conditions. We are approaching the day when all breeding stock will be selected on the basis of performance in terms of both quality of product and economy of production.
Crop protection will probably interest the hon. member for Rosthern. Developments in agriculture have increased and will continue to increase the numbers of pests affecting our domestic crops and animals and their significance in terms of economic losses. This introduces an increasing hazard and degree of gamble into the farmers' operation which can only be eliminated by control of pests, whether insects, diseases or weeds.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
Much of our research has gone into understanding the nature and habits of pests and devising control programs. The control programs have developed to the point where, for example, we can ensure a scab-free apple, or that an epidemic of grasshoppers will not eliminate the cereal or forage crop.
We have a big job ahead of us if we are going to continue to place quality products in the consumer's basket, protect the farmer from wide fluctuations in his income, and at the same time ensure that we do not build up harmful residues in our soils or exceed residue tolerances for pesticides in the consumer diet. Not the least of the problems is the development of resistance in pests to control agents. Thus, we are and will be engaged in controlling pests through breeding resistance into our crops, by introducing biological control agents, by the genetic introduction into the pest of factors limiting the increase of the species, and by developing chemicals more specific to the pests and less hazardous to warm blooded animals such as ourselves.
It is the opinion of the minister and the government that our research stations should be set up in such a way that they will meet the immediate needs of the farmers in the areas which they are intended to serve, and a substantial approach has been made in this general direction.

Surely, if anyone must accept responsibility for a decline in agricultural realized net income during the year 1963, it must be the government which was in power during the period just preceding that decline. After all, the government we have today did not come to office until some time in April, four months after the year had started, and even if they had had a completely new agricultural policy to implement at that time-and I do not think they had one-it would be almost ridiculous to expect that the fruits of such a policy could have been realized during the fiscal year 1963.

C.B.C. that have appeared have suggested that the camera work is erratic and that the film is not up to C.B.C. standards. I want to make the point to the house that the man who did the camera work is the man who did the camera work for the very famous television documentary in the United States that showed the Kennedy brothers facing up to the civil rights situation in Alabama. That particular television film won tremendous acclaim for the fact that it introduced the exciting new technique of the wandering camera and wandering sound. While it gave a sort of uneveness to the film, once the viewer became accustomed to it he felt he was really inside things and it was an exciting experience something like, I suppose, when the first vista screens were introduced in the movie theatres. But this is the man who did the camera work.
Who was the producer? Was he some stumblebum off the streets? As a matter of fact, Mr. Ballentine has a very high reputation as a producer and he has been associated with a number of films that have won international awards. So the producer and the cameraman are people with real reputations. One of the terrible things about what has ensued is that their reputations are under a cloud because for some reason the C.B.C. changed its mind in a period of 12 hours on May 5.
The man who announced the turn-down is a man by the name of Reeves Hagan who is in charge of public affairs for the C.B.C.

Mr. Speaker, when this subject was last before the house I drew the attention of Your Honour and hon. members to the importance of the subject matter to the people of most of the constituencies of the Atlantic provinces. Twenty nine constituencies in the Atlantic provinces are bordered by the Atlantic ocean, and the lives of the people in these constituencies are deeply touched by all matters affecting this great and historic industry, the fishing industry.
Now, as Your Honour knows, the scheme of the legislation is complicated. I know from what has been said by hon. members opposite, particularly by hon. members from that most westerly of our provinces, British Columbia, that there is in that quarter a certain uneasiness with the bill before the house. I think Your Honour should know that this uneasiness is not shared by the people of Atlantic Canada. We think that the scheme of this legislation is excellent. We see in this legislation a pre-figuring of an arrangement which will be highly beneficial both to our inshore fishermen and to those who venture out farther upon the sea.
Your Honour will recall that this legislation provides for the drawing of straight base lines. The waters inside those base lines will be the inland waters of Canada, and all legislation which applies to any of the inland waters of Canada generally will apply there. I think the importance of this aspect sometimes has been overlooked. Outside the straight base lines will be the territorial sea of Canada extending for three miles seaward, and immediately beyond that-

I think anyone who has perused the bill knows that what this bill
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones enables the government to do is to describe a particular sequence of straight lines which will give to Canada the largest possible portion of sea for its use. I do not believe anybody in this house would demand more. I think I know to what the hon. gentleman is adverting in his question, and I shall come to his point later.
As I was saying before I was interrupted, the third aspect concerns Canada's fishing zones. These will lie beyond the territorial sea in a band of water nine miles wide, so that outside the straight base line there will be a 12 mile area for which the fishing regulations made by the government of Canada will be the regulating principles. I think anybody who is familiar with the oculated coast line of Atlantic Canada will appreciate how attractive this legislation is to us.
Now, it has been suggested that this is not the juncture at which this particular bill should have been brought forward. We have been told that it would have been better for the government to have done one of two things, either to have proceeded with those negotiations, which I am sure every hon. member in this house would wish us to conduct with friendly powers, and at the conclusion of those negotiations embalm the result in a statute of parliament, or to proceed by drawing up now a bill to be enacted declaring prior to further negotiations what our base line would be.
I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that neither of these courses of action would be as desirable as the course which the present government has elected to follow. As we know, the question of the rights of other powers to have their fishermen fish in our waters is a complicated one. It is not likely that the governments of other countries will lightly give up any claims which they may make. I do not wish to pass upon the validity of these claims. I am sure that in some instances they may very well be regarded by some of our international lawyers as exaggerated. They make these claims both on treaty grounds and on historic grounds. I think everybody in the house would insist that before taking the definitive action, which this government is prepared to take eventually if necessary, there should be complete and amicable exploration of the claims of these other countries.
This exploration, we have been told, has been under way for several months and can be expected to continue for some time. What the government is now asking for is really very simple. The government is coming to this house and is saying, we want you now to give us a mandate to proceed. We have engaged these other countries in negotiations. The negotiations have proceeded to that point

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones at which we are now prepared to ask parliament to give us a mandate to bring this matter to a successful conclusion. We believe that this negotiation has proceeded to the point at which we should be able to inform those powers with whom we have been negotiating that we indeed have the statutory authority to make a final settlement in this whole complicated affair.
Now, sir, in the circumstances I do not see how any other course of action would have been reasonable. I suspect that even had there been no change in government a year ago, parliament today might very well find itself in exactly the same position that it is in now, and I would hope that hon. members who happen to belong to my party would not in that case chastise the government for coming to parliament at this juncture to ask for a mandate to establish a straight line base system and a 12 mile fishing zone, both of which would be so beneficial to our people.
I have almost concluded, but there is one more thing I want to say. It is that I hope, as the debate proceeds on this important issue, that nothing will be put on the record which will cause any misconception in any quarter, within this country or without this country, as to our determination to establish for Canada a 12 mile fishing zone extending beyond waters which are ours by undoubted right. I think this is something on which, despite our minor disagreements, we are emphatically agreed. I think no one in any quarter should have any doubt about this matter. This is one issue on which the Canadian people are enthusiastically unanimous. We are going to have this. We prefer to have it be achieved by amicable negotiation, but we are going to have it, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any measure dealing with the fishing industry is of vital importance to Canadians generally, and especially to representatives from the Atlantic provinces. I listened with considerable interest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when he made his statement relative to the government's proposal unilaterally to establish a 12 mile exclusive fishing zone off Canada's coasts.
While this action is commendable from a conservation point of view, there are still some questions unanswered, questions that require clarification by the government. The most important question in the minds of many Canadian fishermen today deals with the problem of friendly relations that may or that may not exist between Canada and the United States as a result of the government's action.
On the east coast we are concerned with the preservation of our traditional fisheries 

markets in the United States, markets that are of vital importance to our maritime economy and to our east coast fishing industry. I ask the minister and the government where are the safeguards for these markets? What are the results of the negotiations that have been carried on in recent weeks and months by the Secretary of State for External Affairs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: Are you asking me to answer now?

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: Yes, I would like to have that statement on the record.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
As this is a very important matter I do not want to interfere with my hon. friend making his speech, but he asked the question. As he knows, there are negotiations under way between Canada, the United States, France and a number of other countries. Those negotiations have not concluded and it is because they have not concluded that it has not been possible-as the hon. gentleman who has just spoken indicated-to proceed definitively and completely with the establishment of the straight base line system.
The negotiations are still under way. These negotiations are friendly, and there would be no justification in anything that has taken place for any concern on the part of anyone in Canada about our relations with the United States or with any other countries. We are proceeding as friends in our negotiations.
There is no intention to interfere with the treaty, or historic fishing rights of the United States, with whom the particular negotiation has been put in question by my hon. friend, and there is no justification for creating the suggestion that anything involving Canada's interests stands in jeopardy. Coming as he does from a fishing district I am sure my hon. friend joins with my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) in saying it is desirable that we should have a 12 mile fishing zone to protect our fishing industry.

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
I am grateful to the minister for his explanation, but I would like to tell him that I expressed my concern in the manner, which I did a moment ago, as a result of his very own words which he placed on record in Hansard on May 20 at page 3409, as follows:
I am convinced that in taking this action now- as the government is doing, unilaterally-Canada is acting in accordance with present day international law and practice.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
