speechtext:
The government is convinced that we are following the wisest course in immediately seeking

agreements with the countries affected by our action. We are equally convinced that we must carry forward our negotiations with these countries before we proclaim the base lines for our entire coast.
Then a little further on he stated:
When the government took its decision to establish a 12 mile fishing zone and straight base lines, we did not minimize the problems involved in some of the negotiations lying ahead of us. Nor do we minimize them now. These negotiations may be difficult and we must accept this fact.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: It is because of those words and the very doubts that the minister raised in the minds of many Canadians over the results of these negotiations that I spoke as I did. He states that the government is convinced, but I question whether he has yet convinced the United States who have traditionally rights in these waters. It is in the United States market that we must sell so much of our fish, and this is why I raise this doubt.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: What I am pointing out to my hon. friend is that what the United States are concerned about has nothing to do with markets at all. This is a point of law. It does not in any way involve Canada's markets in the United States. These do not stand in jeopardy at all and the very suggestion that they do, which my hon. friend makes, is one that I suggest to him- as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) pointed out the other night-is not helpful to a very important negotiation under way now between Canada and the United States.

maintopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be the last in the house to say anything that would not be helpful in the negotiations, because I represent a constituency which has undoubtedly the largest fishing fleet in North America, and therefore I want my remarks to be helpful. But when you are dealing with an industry like the fishing industry, that will have a market value in my province of Nova Scotia alone, this year of approximately $70 million, this house and this industry need facts about the protective measures that are being taken for its future.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the place for any fast, slick promises that may have been made during the last two election campaigns by hon. members who now occupy the seats to the right of Your Honour and who form the government, promises made about the value of a 12 mile fishing zone. We in the Atlantic provinces know that conservation measures must be taken, but we are also a practical people and we know that at present some 70 per cent of our entire catch of fish must be sold on the
26. 1964
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones American market. The Lunenburg county fleet alone can catch sufficient fish to feed the entire population of Canada, some 19 million persons.
So I say we need and must maintain the United States market for our fishing industry. In speeches I have made on this subject from the day I entered the house I have taken this stand and I reiterate it tonight because its importance cannot be underestimated. It is for this reason I wish to impress on the minister, for the benefit of thousands of Canadian fishermen and for the benefit of an equal number of processors and handlers of the fish we land on the Atlantic coast, the importance of maintaining this market and assuring us that the Americans are in complete agreement with the negotiations and with the establishment of this limit.
The subject of fisheries conservation is not something new. It is a problem which has plagued various governments since the early days of this century. In fact, we read in a royal commission report on fisheries in 1928- the exact date is May 4-that the following resolution was passed by the House of Commons on February 6, 1911:
That in the opinion of this house, as the mode of fishing known as steam trawling prosecuted by ships of different nationalities on the coast of Canada outside Canadian waters is destructive to fish life, it is expedient in order to conserve the deep sea fisheries, that negotiations be opened wih the view of securing an international agreement-
And you will note it specifically states "international agreement"-
-prohibiting this mode of fishing in such spawning grounds for deep sea fish as the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence and the banks of the north Atlantic adjacent to the coasts of Canada and Newfoundland.
That was way back on February 6, 1911. Then, in the same report on page 91 it is stated:
In order to protect further the shore fishermen, the Canadian government in 1915 enacted a regulation under the Customs Act, whereby the master of any steam-trawier is required before he is granted a clearance for the fishing grounds to give the customs officer a declaration that he will not fish within at least 12 miles from shore, this regulation to apply to all steam-trawlers clearing from a Canadian port on the Atlantic coast. Since that time no further restrictions have been placed on steam-trawlers operating from ports of the maritime provinces.
It is this latter regulation which has plagued the Canadian fishermen over the years and as a result we find the anomalous situation in which Canadian fishermen have, since 1915, been required to fish 12 miles from the Canadian coast while fishermen of all other nations have been permitted to fish within three miles of our shores.
I might add that the three mile limit has never been agreed to among the nations of the

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones world, as far as I can see from the literature I have read. Such a limit was proposed many years ago by two great international powers, Great Britain and the United States, the idea being that the three mile range of their cannon would establish sovereignty over their coastal waters. However, when the league of nations convened a conference at The Hague in 1930 to consider regulations concerning the law of the sea there was so much disagreement on what should be the breadth of territorial water that no resolution or proposal could even be put to a vote. Interest in this matter seemed to lapse until 1958 in which year the United Nations called a conference in Geneva to consider the law of the sea. It was evident that fishing rights and territorial limits had become more important over the years since representatives from 86 states attended the conference. A Conservative government was in power in Canada and under the able leadership of the then minister of external affairs, Hon. Howard Green, a Canadian proposal supporting a 12 mile limit was put forward. Here, again, I pay tribute to the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) for his remarks in commendation of the action taken by Mr. Green at that time. I think it is praiseworthy that the minister should in this way have done justice to one of Canada's great ministers. We put forward at that time a proposal for a 12 mile limit. Our proposal was known as a "six and six" proposal-six miles of territorial sea and six miles in which fishing limits applied. The present proposal calls for a three mile territorial sea and a nine mile fishing zone. In effect, we advocated what we will refer to as a 12 mile limit proposal. We, the Conservatives, hoped to establish this 12 mile limit by international agreement bearing in mind our trade and treaty commitments. We Conservatives believed in international agreement because a principle is at stake in this problem-the principle that the rights of states in international law depend on the consent of other states. However, although the conference was successful in reaching agreement on 113 articles of the law of the sea, after six weeks of intensive debate the contest between those who wished a three mile territorial sea and those who wished a 12 mile territorial sea failed by one vote to gain the required two thirds majority which would have resolved it. Accordingly, there is still no agreement on the breadth of the territorial sea among the 86 nations represented at that conference.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-BASIS FOR FIGURES RESPECTING NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
LABOUR CONDITIONS-BASIS FOR FIGURES RESPECTING NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raise tonight concerns an item published in the newspaper Mont-real-Matin on May 20, 1964, and entitled: "Who is right?" I quote:
The number of claimants of unemployment benefits reached 597,000 on March 31, according to the d.b.s. official unemployment statistics showed 403,000 unemployed throughout Canada on April 18.
The discrepancy between those two figures, the former based on reports of the unemployment insurance commission, and the latter on a sample survey, has never been clearly explained.
As a preliminary to the question which I directed on May 20, 1964 to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), I quoted the figures which had appeared in the article of the said newspaper.
The question read as follows:
Could the minister clearly explain the discrepancy between the two figures, since one is based on a report of the unemployment insurance commission and the other on a sample survey.
By computing the difference between the figures provided by the unemployment insurance commission and those of the sample survey, we obtain the rather interesting and high figure of 194,000 unemployed over or below, whether we refer to one of the official sources concerning unemployment.

How can a reduction of 194,000 unemployed in Canada within 15 days be explained?
The sixty days of the present Liberal government having proved to be a disaster for the whole Canadian population, could it be that they were offset by the first 15 days of April, during which the government would have created all the jobs promised during the election campaign?
I doubt very much, Mr. Speaker, that we have there the explanation for this tremendous gap.
Where then are we to find the answer to that question? We might have to look for it in the meaning or definition given to the word "unemployed".
What is meant by "unemployed"? Is it only those who are lucky enough to get unemployment insurance benefits, that is to say, if I may, those unemployed on a full-time basis, who are not allowed to have a little sideline and earn a little money without always feeling the sword of Damocles hanging above their heads and which might come crashing down the moment it is discovered that they are earning a few cents on top of their unemployment insurance benefits?
On the other hand, is the word "unemployed" used to mean those who, while drawing their unemployment insurance benefits, in whole or in part, can earn a maximum amount of money during the week? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that some people can earn up to $20 a week without this being detrimental to them as far as their collection of unemployment insurance benefits is concerned. I do not believe that they draw those benefits in full but they draw at least an important portion of the benefits due to their condition. These people are usually classified as part-time workers.
Could the minister tell us whether, in computing the number of unemployed registered at the various offices, the statistics officers consider as unemployed those people I just mentioned or described?
Finally, are investigations made to establish the number of persons unemployed, many of whom, knowing they have no chance at all of being put on the list of unemployed who get unemployment insurance benefits, do not even try to get on that list?
Finally, are those who are denied during two or even six weeks, unemployment insurance benefits as a penalty for their failure to follow the required procedure at their local unemployment insurance office, included as unemployed?
In that last case, I could say that if those people are not considered as unemployed, we
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion must blame certain little aristocrats who, sitting behind their desk, are making game of those poor people who do not understand that awkward unemployment insurance legislation. They go back home with empty hands simply because they were taken in by those little squirts who sometimes interpret the act as they please to save the government the payment of too many benefits.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I should like to know what, in the opinion of the minister, is an unemployed and second, why there is such a discrepancy in the official figures from the unemployment insurance commission and the d.b.s.
I should like the Minister of Labour, who as I notice now is absent tonight to explain to me those figures.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-BASIS FOR FIGURES RESPECTING NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) has asked me to express his regret at his inability to be in the house this evening at this period. The hon. member has introduced several more questions which of course it would be impossible for me, or for anyone else for that matter, to answer within the three minutes provided under the new rule. However, I point out to the hon. member that he has answered some of these questions himself.
In order to explain the discrepancy in the two figures I would first refer the hon. member to a report of the committee on unemployment statistics that was set up by the former administration, which committee reported to the house in August of 1960. Briefly, Mr. Speaker, I would simply state that the 597,300 active unemployment insurance claimants reported by the unemployment insurance commission as of March 31 include those persons referred to by the hon. member who are employed part-time but do receive some measure of benefit.
The dominion bureau of statistics labour force survey, on the other hand, of April 18 as opposed to the earlier date of March 31, does not include such persons. In addition, the unemployment insurance figures provided by the unemployment insurance commission are an average of the number of people drawing benefit during the whole month, while the d.b.s. figures are an estimate of the number of people unemployed during the third week of the month; that is to say, ending the 18th day. The 194,300 discrepancy may be further explained, or rather is self-evident, when one has regard for the significant dates when employment seasonally increases at an accelerated rate.

maintopic: TRADE-CONTINUATION OF POLICY RESPECTING OIL EXPORTS
TRADE-CONTINUATION OF POLICY RESPECTING OIL EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 21 last I asked a question which is to be found at page 3431 of Hansard. I want to make it very clear that when I mentioned that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) was absent that day, I know he had absolute justification for being absent; he was no doubt engaged in duties in reference to his own department even if he was not in the house. Therefore I directed my question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The question was in reference to an article-I do not want to take the time of the house by reading from the newspaper-which appeared in the New York Times and was requoted in the Calgary Herald. I read it in both newspapers. The article was in reference to the petroleum industry, and in particular concerned the acceptance by the Soviet union of petroleum and other oil products in return for Canadian grain. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said that there was no justification for the statement. His actual words were:
Not to my knowledge, but it is important, Mr. Speaker, and I shall look into it.
The next day, May 22, and I am not criticizing the Prime Minister because only a day had elapsed, I asked him if he had any information. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) had not returned from his duties elsewhere and the Prime Minister said he had no information but he again emphasized that it was an important question.
I am not complaining about the answer given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce at all but I had a supplementary question I wished to ask because if we did get into a deal with Soviet Russia in petroleum products there would be repercussions from the United States. Even before the minister became a member of the house he was no doubt active in the enterprise when he was deputy minister of trade and commerce, and we know that the eastern market is open to the entry of Venezuelan crude. In this case these companies are United States companies. If we introduced quotas for the eastern market there would be repercussions in the United States.

I think this is a very important question. It may be that I owe the Speaker some apology for the way I spoke the other afternoon when he brought me to order, but with the greatest respect to you, Mr. Speaker, it is an important, urgent question, and in saying that I have in mind some of the other questions asked that day. When we realize that a year ago we were able to bring our payments position closer to balancing because of the petroleum industry may I say I was rather shocked when I was prevented from asking this question.
We can look at the Canada Year Book for 1962 and 1963 particularly, and I am sure the minister will not have any argument in that regard. I am not saying this because the Conservatives were in power then. I want to keep this matter out of politics. It is too important to get it into politics. It affects the economy of western Canada. A national oil policy was developed whereby we could ship our crude petroleum to the western states. Discussions were carried on with the proper authorities in the United States and their purchases of our crude petroleum were beginning to accelerate. The only way we can keep the oil industry of western Canada healthy is either by consuming the product domestically or exporting up to 800,000 barrels of crude petroleum a day. The Canada Year Book will show that we brought our exports up to 668,000 barrels daily. In other words, we were near the target.
Prior to the Suez crisis we had trouble. Then the Suez crisis came along and we were able to accelerate our exports and to keep our petroleum industry healthy. But then we got into trouble after the Suez crisis ended. We then went downgrade and we got into a serious situation indeed. Since the deal made in 1959 or 1960-I am not too sure what year -whereby the western states would buy crude petroleum from western Canada and we would leave the eastern market alone our industry has been fairly healthy. So I felt that my supplementary question was very important.
I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that if we did enter into a deal with Soviet Russia in respect of crude petroleum there would be repercussions in the United States that would cramp our whole industry and bring about a serious depression in the industry, not only in western Canada but throughout Canada as a whole. The repercussions would not only be felt in the industry but in respect of our balance of payments position with the United States.
When you prevented my asking a supplementary question of that calibre and importance, Mr. Speaker, and allowed other

questions of lesser calibre and with really no national importance, then it was only natural that I should want to take up the matter at this time. I am not criticizing the minister's answer to my question. He said there was no truth in the statement and that they were merely negotiating. There is nothing wrong with negotiating as long as the government of Canada, whether Liberal or Conservative, does not bite.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: TRADE-CONTINUATION OF POLICY RESPECTING OIL EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) for giving me an opportunity of saying one or two things about our national oil policy. If I may refer to the question the hon. member did ask, I shall quote from page 3536 of Hansard for May 25, 1964:
Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce continuing the national oil policy so that we may accelerate our exports in this field to a target of approximately 800,000 barrels of crude petroleum a day, taking into account the amount we use domestically?
I am sure my hon. friend does not read all my speeches, but perhaps I may refer him to a speech I made in Calgary on February 3 in which I said, amongst other things, that I agreed with the national oil policy which had been enunciated by the previous government. I agreed that this was a good policy. I went on to say that as soon as possible after this government took office I made clear that this policy would be continued and carried forward.
I then went on to say in the concluding part of this speech that I thought it was necessary to establish new targets. At that time I said I thought it was feasible and desirable to establish a target figure for 1964. I quote from that speech:
After considering the prospects for growth in the domestic market, for additional displacement by Canadian oil in the Ontario market, and for exports, we think average production should reach about 850,000 barrels per day.
I think my hon. friend would like to know that production for the first two months of this year was well in excess of this target, so that the figure of 800,000 barrels he somehow considers fairly satisfactory has been well exceeded. It seems to me that the industry is well within reach of the target, looking at the whole of the year, but to achieve it the industry will have to exert strong and continued efforts to supply Ontario west of the Ottawa valley with products of refined Canadian crude. I feel confident that the industry will do this and achieve its objective.

CROWN ASSETS-DISPOSITION OF EQUIPMENT OF CLOSED RADAR STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury) because, within a week, it is the second time that he is here for this question period between 10 and 10.30 in the evening to consider the matter of the radar station in St. Sylvestre.
That name has become quite familiar to the ears of hon. members and they are all aware that this famous station is located in the riding of Lotbiniere.
Mr. Speaker, here is the matter I want to call to the attention of the minister in his capacity as Minister of Defence Production: there is in St. Sylvestre some material and equipment worth quite a lot of money and I would like to know what the Minister of Defence Production intends to do with it.
Is the minister willing to dispose of that material and equipment which would not have any military use and, in such a case, is he willing to set what I would call a nominal price for it, in order to stimulate the interest of the industrialists or other people who might be interested in operating the existing facilities?
The minister is aware, I think, that an association that goes by the name of "Centre d'initiative de Saint-Sylvestre" was created recently. It is made up of the following members: the mayor of the parish of St. Sylvestre, Mr. Ondsime Nappert, a well known citizen because last year he won the title of maple king of the province of Quebec, Messrs. Henri Dion, Andre Huppe, Edouard Cotter, Arthur Barbeau, Louis R. Ruel, Paul Th6-berge, Yvan Dallaire, of Levis, and Gaston Blais, of Lauzon, who would like to set up a recreation centre in St. Sylvestre.
That project is just as good as any other, and if the minister were willing to sell all the equipment at St. Sylvestre for a reasonable price, I am sure that that would encourage some organization to operate that centre for the welfare of the people who live in the riding of Lotbiniere, who enjoyed a certain prosperity after the establishment of the radar station. In fact, the closing down of that station is causing some worry, and that is why I insist so often on this subject in the house. That is why I spare no effort to convince the minister of the urgency of maintaining the local economy at the level it reached because of the radar station.
I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Defence Production is a man of great honesty and competence. If I speak of honesty, it is because, at one time, some people expressed

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the fear that the disposal of equipment by the Minister of Defence Production might lead to speculation. We must prevent that, and if the government is willing to get rid of the equipment in question, I hope it will do so to the advantage of the St. Sylvestre area and in such a way as to prevent certain financiers, who always find a way to profit from such situations, from running off with everything. The proposed centre would be quite advantageous for the residents of St. Sylvestre, since the radar station is in the immediate neighbourhood. That is the question I wanted to put to the minister. I thank him for his kindness, since this is the second time he comes to the house to speak about St. Sylvestre during this period.

I wish to commend the hon. member for his suggestion that the equipment of the radar station be turned over to an initiative centre.
